---
title: "C: Cardiovascular system"
description: "ATC group C covers the heart and blood vessels: drugs for heart failure and arrhythmias, blood pressure drugs, diuretics, and cholesterol lowering drugs."
date: "2026-02-08"
---

Group C holds the drugs that act on the heart and the blood vessels, together with the drugs that lower cholesterol and other lipids in the blood.

|  | Description | In plain terms | Example drug |
| ---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **C01** | Cardiac therapy | drugs acting directly on the heart | Amiodarone (C01BD01) / digoxin (C01AA05) |
| **C02** | Antihypertensives |  | Methyldopa (C02AB01), doxazosin (C02CA04). Most other blood pressure drugs sit in C03, C07, C08 and C09. |
| **C03** | Diuretics |  | Furosemide (C03CA01) / spironolactone (C03DA01) |
| **C04** | Peripheral vasodilators | widen arteries in the arms and legs | Naftidrofuryl (C04AX21), pentoxifylline (C04AD03). |
| **C05** | Vasoprotectives | for hemorrhoids, varicose veins, fragile capillaries | Topical hydrocortisone (C05AA01) for hemorrhoids; diosmin (C05CA03), a capillary stabilizing agent. |
| **C07** | Beta blocking agents |  | Bisoprolol (C07AB07) / metoprolol (C07AB02) |
| **C08** | Calcium channel blockers |  | Amlodipine (C08CA01) / diltiazem (C08DB01) |
| **C09** | Agents acting on the renin-angiotensin system | blood-pressure hormone system: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) | Ramipril (C09AA05) / candesartan (C09CA06) |
| [**C10**](c10/) | Lipid modifying agents | cholesterol- and triglyceride-lowering drugs | Atorvastatin (C10AA05) / rosuvastatin (C10AA07) |

: ATC C level 2 codes {#tbl-atc-c-lvl-2 tbl-colwidths="[9, 29, 26, 36]"}

## Blood pressure

For the antihypertensives in C02, C03, C07, C08 and C09, efficacy is measured as the fall in blood pressure [@johnston1992doseresponse].
Cardiovascular outcomes, such as stroke and heart attack (myocardial infarction), are clinical events, analyzed as time to event [@holfordTimeEventTutorial2013].

Blood pressure is a continuous measurement, and a monitor worn during daily life (ambulatory monitor) can repeat it many times over 24 hours.
In a population analysis of moxonidine (C02AC05), the 24-hour profiles of one of its two studies held 74 to 99 measurements each.
Two cosine terms described the circadian rhythm in the baseline, and this baseline model was combined with an E~max~ model for the drug effect, with an effect compartment for the delay [@hempel1998].

In patients with heart failure given moxonidine, the effects on systolic blood pressure and heart rate lagged behind the plasma concentration, and were also described with an effect compartment.
The concentration giving half the maximal effect (EC~50~) rose over the 12 weeks of treatment [@brynne2001].

Francheteau and colleagues built a closed-loop model of cardiovascular regulation, in which a control variable representing mainly the pressure-sensing reflex of the arteries (baroreceptor reflex) responds to changes in mean arterial pressure.
In it, the calcium channel blocker nicardipine (C08CA04) lowered the resistance of the blood vessels to flow (total peripheral resistance).
Together with the feedback loop, this described the time course of both the blood flow pumped by the heart (cardiac output) and mean arterial pressure after intravenous infusion in healthy volunteers [@francheteau1993].

### Baseline and placebo

In 255 subjects given placebo or one of five types of antihypertensive drug, the fall in systolic blood pressure correlated with the initial blood pressure in every group.
In the subset analyzed with concentration-effect models, the sensitivity to the drug also correlated with the initial blood pressure [@sumner1988].

Across the placebo arms of 52 trials in non-resistant hypertension, systolic blood pressure fell by 5.9 mm Hg.
The fall was larger in trials with a higher baseline blood pressure [@patel2015placebo].

## Dose finding

Several antihypertensive drugs were introduced at doses that were too high, among them most thiazide diuretics, propranolol (C07AA05), atenolol (C07AB03) and captopril (C09AA01).
These doses usually came from studies that raised the dose at regular intervals until the desired effect or unacceptable adverse effects appeared.
The starting doses were often too high, and the intervals between dose steps too short.
In many cases the high doses caused unnecessary adverse effects, such as the biochemical effects of thiazide diuretics, and taste disturbances and a shortage of neutrophil white blood cells (neutropenia) with captopril.
Johnston recommended parallel-group designs with single doses, and with enough statistical power to separate the upper and lower ends of the dose-response curve [@johnston1992doseresponse].
Good practices for exposure-response analyses of clinical endpoints, which support such dose decisions, are set out in a tutorial [@overgaardEstablishingGoodPractices2015].

## Covariates

For furosemide (C03CA01), a review compares pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in health and in a range of diseases [@hammarlund1989furosemide].
When covariates are selected stepwise and only the statistically significant ones are kept, the covariate model risks selection bias, and correlated covariates add to it and cost power [@ribbing2004covariate].
